title: She Retired to Care for Family. New Food-Aid Rules Got in the Way
summary: Lisa Reese worked for nearly 40 years — at a liquor store, cleaning apartments, and in hospitality. She never received government assistance. Then, at 62, she retired to care for her family. Now new work rules for food aid have complicated that plan. Reese lives in Capitol Heights, Maryland, in her family's longtime home. Three generations live there now. Her 80-year-old mother is in senior living. She shares the house with her uncle, who has had surgery for liver cancer, and with her daughter and 2-year-old granddaughter, whom she helps care for. Daycare was expensive, she said, so she decided to retire to take care of everybody. Reese spent the past 25 years at Marriott, working the front desk, room service, and events. After leaving her job, living mainly on Social Security was tough. Prices kept rising, and one gas bill reached $500. This summer, Reese was approved for a small amount from the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, known as SNAP. To get $63 a month in food aid, she must work, train, or volunteer for 80 hours a month. The requirement is part of sweeping changes to SNAP and Medicaid in the One Big Beautiful Bill, signed by President Trump last year. The law expanded work rules to include people aged 55 to 64. The Department of Agriculture, which oversees SNAP, said the work expectation is not punishment and should be applauded, not used as scare tactics. Reese meets the rule by volunteering at Mission of Love Charities, a nonprofit near her home that helps people who are homeless or low-income. On a recent day, she packed snack bags for people who would line up later. Her four-hour morning shift lets her watch her granddaughter in the afternoons, and she says the work makes her feel good.
why_it_matters: Food aid rules decide whether people who care for family full time can still get help buying food. The story shows how a change in one rule can reshape daily life for retirees and the families who depend on them.

background_read: SNAP, the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, is a government program that helps people with low incomes buy food.
Some people who receive SNAP must meet work rules, which means working, training, or volunteering for a set number of hours each month to keep their food aid.
Social Security is a government program that pays monthly money to retired workers and others, and for some people it is their main income after they stop working.
When the rules for a program change, people who depend on it, including older adults caring for family, may have to change their plans to keep receiving help.
